en: Homage to the Omniscient One.

Having first prostrated before the foremost in the world, who has crossed over the abode of suffering and reached the infinite further shore, I shall open the jewel-treasury of the training precepts of the Omniscient One in the midst of the assembly of noble ones. (1)

He whose banner of fame is renowned throughout the three worlds, who has let out the lion’s roar that proclaims the true Dharma, who has exhausted all the treasuries of jewels, and whose feet are rubbed by the crest-jewels of the cosmic egg. // 2 //
This Prātimokṣa is said to be the foundation, the heart, and the essence of the entire, unfathomable, and boundless ocean of the Buddha’s Vinaya. (3)
This is the collection of the written scriptures of the King of the True Dharma;
this is the merchant guild of monks, whose great market is the merchandise of the training rules.
This is the medicine that neutralizes the poison of those corrupted by immorality;
this is the goad for the elephant-like youths who are bewildered by their youth.
This is the boat for crossing the ocean-deep saṃsāra;
this is the path for conquering the afflictions, the foremost leader of the king.
He stands like a root staircase for ascending to the city of liberation;
even after I have attained nirvana, he shall be extolled as your Teacher.
Having himself diligently subdued both the agitated and the unagitated,
Samantabhadra, with his senses stilled, [attained] complete peace.
The Prātimokṣa is never to be recited by those who have not been initiated; it is always to be guarded by monks who desire liberation.
Even when one has been conquered, they act for one's detriment;
even when one has rendered assistance, they seek to do harm.
Hearing the Prātimokṣa is difficult to obtain even in ten million eons; its grasping, its retention, and likewise its transgression are extremely difficult to find. (8)
The arising of Buddhas is happiness; the proclamation of the Dharma is happiness; the harmony of the Saṅgha is happiness; and the austerity of the śramaṇas is happiness. // 9 //
Happy is the sight of the noble ones, and dwelling together with the virtuous is also happy;
by not seeing fools, there would be constant happiness. // 10 //
It is a joy to see those who possess moral virtue; it is a joy to see those who are deeply learned;
and it is a joy to see Arhats who are fully liberated from rebirth. // 11 //
Happy is the river, happy is the ford, and happy is the birth of one who has conquered through the Dharma;
happy indeed is the attainment of wisdom, for the destruction of the conceit "I am" is happiness. (12)
Happy indeed is the dwelling of those who have made their resolve, whose senses are conquered, and who are deeply learned;
they have reached old age in peaceful forests, having extinguished their youth within the woods. (13)
"Venerable ones, the summer retreat has ended; only this much remains.
Life passes away, and old age and death have arrived.
The teaching of the Teacher is being transgressed."

"Venerable ones, you must apply yourselves with heedfulness; for it is through heedfulness that the awakening of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones was attained. Such are the wholesome qualities conducive to awakening.
What need has the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples for further duties? Their purpose is small and their tasks are few."
"Venerable sirs, announce the purity of intent for those who have not yet arrived, and inform us when it has been announced.
Having bowed to the Lion of the Śākyas and having placed my hands joined in reverence before him, I shall proclaim the Prātimokṣa; may he hear this Vinaya from us. (14)
And having heard this, you should act here exactly as it was taught by the Great Seer; you must be diligent regarding even the slightest faults. (15)

And he who, with effort, swiftly and constantly directs the horse of the mind toward his words and speech, by means of the Prātimokṣa bridle—which is like a hundred sharp thorns—with which it is thoroughly pierced. (16)
Those human steeds who do not turn back from their respective shares at the mere word of the Great-Souled One will indeed be victors in the battle against the afflictions. // 17 //
But those for whom this bridle does not exist, nor even internal desire, they will wander wildly, being crushed by the battle of the afflictions. (19)
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha. Today is the Poṣadha of the Saṃgha, being either the fourteenth or the fifteenth day.
If it seems timely to the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha consent and permit that the Saṃgha perform the Poṣadha and recite the exposition of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra. This is the motion.
Venerable sirs, we shall perform the Poṣadha; we shall recite the exposition of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra."
Whoever has committed an offense must disclose it;
if there is no offense, one should remain silent.
And by means of this silence, we shall know that the Venerable Ones are pure.
Just as an individual monk who is questioned gives his answer, even so, in such an assembly of monks, there is a formal proclamation up to three times.
Furthermore, if a monk, when such a proclamation has been made up to three times in such an assembly of monks, does not disclose an existing offense while being mindful, he commits a deliberate lie.
Indeed, venerable ones, a deliberate lie has been declared by the Blessed One to be an obstructive factor.
Therefore, a monk who remembers that he has committed an offense and desires purification must disclose that offense.
Once it has been disclosed, he finds ease; once it has not been disclosed, he does not find ease.
Venerable sirs, I have indeed recited the introduction to the recitation of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra.
In this regard, I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this matter? A second time, and a third time, I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
Since there is silence, Venerable Ones, I shall thus hold it to be so.
The four *pārājika* rules.
Indeed, venerable sirs, these four *pārājika* rules come up for recitation every half-month in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
Pār.1 (PrMoSū_Mū-Banerjee)

Furthermore, whichever monk, having entered upon the training and the mode of life of the monks, without renouncing the training and without disclosing his weakness in the training, practices unchaste sexual intercourse—
even with an animal— this monk also is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.
Pārājika 2: Should any monk, whether in a village or in the forest, take what belongs to others and has not been given to him, such that it is considered theft,
and for which kind of taking of what is not given a king or a royal official, having seized him, would execute him, bind him, or banish him—
Or if he should speak to him thus: "O man, you are a thief, you are a fool, you are a robber"—
if a monk should take such an ungiven thing,
this monk also becomes one who has committed a defeat (pārājika) and is no longer in communion.
Pārājika 3: Should any monk, with his own hand and intentionally, deprive a human being or one who has the form of a human being of life;
or should he provide them with a weapon, or seek out a weapon-bearer for them; or should he incite them to death, or praise the beauty of death; [he commits an offense involving expulsion].
And he should speak to him thus: "O man, what is the use of this wretched, impure, and miserable life of yours?

O man, death is better for you than life. With such thoughts and intentions approved by his own mind, he should in many ways incite him toward death, or describe the praises of death to him; and if, as a result of that, he should die, this—

Furthermore, a monk who—without knowing, without understanding, and without it being true or existing—claims a superhuman state beyond the reach of ordinary men, becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion. Pār. 4 (PrMoSū_Mū-Banerjee).
If a noble one should claim to have attained a specific realization, knowledge, vision, or a state of dwelling in comfort, saying, "I know this;

I see this," and later—whether being questioned or not—being found to have fallen into such a state, he would look for purification and say: "Venerable sirs, not knowing, I said that I knew; not seeing, I said that I saw. It was empty and vain."
False speech, except out of conceit— this monk also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.
Venerable ones, I have recited the four *pārājika* rules,
by the transgression of any one of which a monk does not obtain communion or shared resources with the monks, being neither before nor after as he was previously.
He becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.
Therefore, I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?
A second time, and a third time, I ask: Are you pure in this matter?

The Venerable Ones are pure in this matter, since they are silent; thus do I understand it. These, indeed, Venerable Ones, are the thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa rules that come up for recitation in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month.
SA.1 Intentionally emitting semen, except during sleep, is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. SA.2 [Continuation of the rule.]
Furthermore, if a monk, with a mind transformed by lust, should engage in physical contact with a woman—
whether by taking her hand, or taking her arm, or taking hold of her hair, or by touching any other major or minor limb,
or by embracing her body— it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

SA.3. Furthermore, if a monk, with a mind corrupted by lust, should address a woman with wicked, sinful, vulgar speech connected to sexual intercourse— just as a young man would address a young woman—
that is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
SA.4.
Furthermore, if a monk, with a mind corrupted by lust, should in the presence of a woman praise his own personal service, saying:
"O sister, this is the foremost of all services, namely, that one serves a monk like me who is virtuous," [he commits a *pāyantika* offense].
One should attend upon a virtuous practitioner of the holy life with this practice, namely, that which is connected with sexual intercourse; this is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

Furthermore, whichever monk should act as a go-between, conveying a man’s intent to a woman, or a woman’s intent to a man, whether for marriage or for a lover, even if only for a momentary occasion, [this is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense].
Saṃghāvaśeṣa:
SA.6 (PrMoSū_Mū-Banerjee) A monk who builds a hut himself, having requested [materials], should have it built without an owner and for his own use, and the hut must be of the prescribed dimensions.
In this regard, the measurement of the hut is twelve spans of the Sugata’s span in length and seven internally in width.
That monk must have other monks brought along to inspect the site;
the site inspected by those monks must be one that involves no construction and has sufficient space around it.
If a monk, on a site that involves injury to living beings and lacks sufficient space, should have a small hut built for himself by his own request— without an owner and intended for his own use—
and if he does not lead other monks to inspect the site, or if the site is not inspected by the monks led there, and he exceeds the prescribed measurement, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Furthermore, when a monk is having a large dwelling built for the Saṅgha with a patron, that monk must have other monks informed for the purpose of inspecting the site.
Once those monks have been brought there, the site must be inspected to ensure it is free from obstacles and has sufficient space around it.

If a monk, having caused a large monastery to be built on a site involving new construction and lacking a walkway, does not lead the monks who are its owners and intended for the Saṅgha to inspect the site, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
(SA.8) Furthermore, if a monk, out of malice and with a premeditated intent, should groundlessly defame a pure monk with a *pārājika* offense, [it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense]. (SA.9)

"Perhaps I might cause him to fall from his celibacy. Later, whether being interrogated or not being interrogated, his own case turns out to be entirely groundless; yet the monk persists in his malice, saying, "I spoke thus out of hatred. This is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

SA.9: Should any monk, out of malice and with an unpleased mind, having taken up some trivial pretext as a mere pretext for another legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) that belongs to a different category, falsely accuse a pure monk of an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*);

"May I indeed cause him to fall away from the religious life"— if, at a later time, when he is being questioned or not being questioned, that legal case turns out to concern something else entirely, and he has grasped some minor point of the Dharma merely by way of a pretext, and the monk persists in his malice, saying, "I spoke thus out of hatred," it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

SA.10 (PrMoSū_Mū-Banerjee) Furthermore, if a monk should strive for the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha, and should persist in maintaining and upholding a legal dispute conducive to causing a schism, that monk is to be addressed by the monks as follows:
— Do not, O Venerable One, strive for the schism of the harmonious Saṃgha, nor persist in maintaining and upholding a legal dispute that leads to such a schism.
Let the Venerable One be reconciled with the Saṃgha; let the Saṃgha be united, in harmony, in agreement, without dispute, and devoted to the teaching of the Dharma with one-pointed focus.
"Being as one with milk and water in harmony, demonstrating the Teacher's [teaching], and dwelling in pleasant contact—renounce this, O Venerable One!
This is the matter that causes a schism in the Saṃgha.
If, when the monks speak thus to that monk, he persists in taking up and adhering to that very matter, [he is one who causes a schism].

If he is pure, it is well that he should relinquish [the offense]; but if he does not relinquish it, he should be questioned and instructed a second and even a third time for the sake of relinquishing that matter. If, being questioned and instructed a second and even a third time, he relinquishes that matter, it is well; but if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
SA.11 Now, if that monk should have companions who speak divisively— whether one, two, or many—
and they should say to those monks: "Venerable sirs, do not [speak of] that monk as being either good or evil."
Or whatever he says, for what reason? Because, venerable sirs, that monk speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya;
he speaks having taken up our will and our preference.
That monk speaks knowing [the truth] and not unknowingly; and what is pleasing and acceptable to this monk is also pleasing and acceptable to us.
Those monks should be addressed by the other monks as follows: "Venerable ones, do not speak thus.

That monk does not speak according to the Dharma, nor does he speak according to the Vinaya; he speaks having taken up what is contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya, following our own desire and preference. That monk speaks without knowing, and what he approves of and endorses is that which he himself knows."
And it does not please you, venerable sir, that there should be a schism in the Saṃgha; nor does it please the venerable ones that there should be a schism in the Saṃgha.

Let the venerable ones be reconciled with the Saṃgha, for the Saṃgha is harmonious, living in mutual joy, without dispute, with a single focus on the teaching of the Dharma, unified like milk and water, manifesting the Teacher’s instructions, and dwelling in comfort.
"Stay, O Venerable One; do not persist in causing a schism in the Saṅgha. Abandon this kind of talk that leads to a schism in the Saṅgha.

Thus should those monks be exhorted and instructed by the monks two or even three times for the sake of relinquishing that matter. Being exhorted and instructed two or even three times, they should relinquish it.
If they do not thus desist, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Should a number of monks dwell in dependence upon a certain village or town, and they should be corrupters of families and of evil conduct, such that their corrupted families are seen [to have been ruined]—
Or if they are heard of, or if they are known—those monks should be addressed by the other monks as follows: "Venerable ones, you are corrupters of families and of evil conduct;
your corruption of families is seen, heard, and known, and so too is yours."
"Evil conduct is seen, heard, and even known among you; depart, venerable sirs, from this residence; enough of your staying here.
If those monks should say to them, "Venerable sirs, these monks act out of favoritism; they act out of hatred..."
"Because they proceed out of delusion and proceed out of fear, they expel some monks from such an offense while not expelling others.
In that case, the monks should be addressed thus: "Venerable ones, do not speak in this way."
Some monks, being driven by favoritism, hatred, delusion, and fear, expel some monks from such an offense while not expelling others.
For what reason? It is because these monks are not driven by favoritism, hatred, delusion, and fear; rather, it is the venerable ones who are so driven.
"You are corrupters of families and practitioners of evil conduct; your families are seen to be corrupted and heard to be so, and your evil practices are seen, heard, and known.
Monks, you venerable ones are swayed by desire, swayed by hatred, swayed by delusion, and swayed by fear—renounce such talk as this!"

Those monks should be addressed by the other monks as follows: "If they should relinquish [this], that is well; if they do not relinquish it, they should be examined and instructed a second and a third time for the sake of relinquishing it. If, being examined and instructed a second and a third time, they should relinquish it, that is well."
If they do not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Here, some monk may be of a difficult-to-speak-to nature regarding the training rules included in the recitation and included in the discourses of the Sugata.

When being addressed by the monks in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, he makes himself unaccountable, saying: "Venerable sirs, do not say anything to me, whether good or bad; nor shall I say anything to the venerable ones, whether good or bad. Let the venerable ones desist from speaking to me, and I too shall desist from speaking to you."

That monk should be addressed by the monks as follows: "Venerable one, when you are being spoken to in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya by the monks regarding the training rules included in the recitation and included in the Sugata’s discourses, you make yourself un-reprovable; Venerable one, let yourself be made reprovable, for the monks are speaking to you in accordance with the Dharma."

Let the Venerable One speak to the monks with accordance to the Dharma and accordance to the Vinaya; let the Venerable One also speak to the monks with accordance to the Dharma and accordance to the Vinaya. For such is the assembly of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, namely, that it consists of mutual admonition and mutual restoration from offenses.
Therefore, O Venerable One, do not make yourself one who is beyond admonition.

That monk should be addressed by the monks in this way: "If he relinquishes that matter, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, he should be formally questioned and instructed a second and a third time for the sake of its relinquishment. If, after being formally questioned and instructed a second and a third time, he relinquishes it..."
If he thinks, "This is a real thing," and does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Venerable ones, I have recited the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules:

nine that entail immediate offense upon commission and four that require a third admonition. If a monk has committed any one of these rules and knowingly conceals it for as long as he does so, for that duration he must—though unwillingly—[undergo penance].
He must undergo the parivāsa probation.
A monk who has completed the parivāsa probation unintentionally must further practice the mānatva penance for six nights before the Saṃgha.

Once the monk has performed the mānatva and is ready for the āvarhaṇa (rehabilitation), having fulfilled the required duties and satisfied the minds of the Bhikṣu-saṃgha, he should go to a place where there is a community of twenty monks; there that monk—
He is to be rehabilitated.

If a community of monks consisting of fewer than twenty members should rehabilitate that monk, that monk is not truly rehabilitated and those monks are to be censured; this is the rule in such a case.
Therefore, I ask the venerable ones: "Are you all pure in this matter?"
A second and even a third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? Since there is silence, Venerable Ones, I consider you to be pure here. III. There are two undetermined rules.
Indeed, these two undetermined rules (*aniyata-dharma*) come up for recitation every half-month in the *Prātimokṣasūtra*.
Aniy.1:
If a monk should sit down in secret, in a concealed place, on a seat with a woman alone, one-on-one, in a manner suitable for sexual desire;
If a female lay follower whose word is trustworthy should charge him with one or another of three categories of offenses— either a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*,

or a *pāyattika* offense— and the monk admits to the sitting, he is to be dealt with according to one or another of those three categories of offenses: either as a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*.
Or rather, whatever legal procedure a female lay follower of trustworthy speech may state regarding that monk, by that very legal procedure must that monk be dealt with; this rule is indefinite.
(Aniyata 2)
Furthermore, if a monk should sit down in private on a concealed seat with a woman, one-on-one, where they are capable of sexual intercourse,
and if a trustworthy female lay follower accuses him of either of two offenses— either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika* offense—
the monk, by admitting to having sat down, is charged with either of those two offenses, namely a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Whether it be by means of a *pāyantika* offense or whatever else a trustworthy female lay follower (*śrāddheyavacanopāsikā*) may accuse that monk of according to the rule, that monk must be dealt with according to that very rule; this rule, too, is indefinite (*aniyata*). "Venerable sirs, I have recited the two indefinite rules."
In this regard, I ask the Venerable Ones: "Is everyone here pure?
A second time and a third time I ask: "Is everyone here pure?
Since there is silence, the Venerable Ones are pure in this matter; thus do I understand it to be.
The thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyantika* rules:
Venerable ones, these thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyantika* rules indeed come up for recitation every half-month in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
NP.1 (PrMoSū_Mū-Banerjee)

When a robe has been finished and the *kaṭhina* has been suspended, a monk may keep an extra robe that has not been formally assigned for a maximum of ten days; if he should keep it longer than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (NP.2).

Furthermore, when a monk has finished his robes and the *kaṭhina* has been suspended, if he should dwell apart from any one of his three robes outside the boundary even for a single night, except with the consent of the Saṃgha, [he commits an offense].
[By means of the formal agreement of the Saṃgha: This is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

(NP.3) When a monk whose robe has been finished and for whom the *kaṭhina* has been suspended, should an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*) arise and he desires it, that monk must accept that robe; having accepted it, if it is completed [as a set],...

Having made it, one must wear it immediately. If it is not completed, that monk must set aside that robe for at most one month while there is still hope of obtaining a robe; he may complete what is deficient. If he sets it aside for longer than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyantika).
NP.4 (PrMoSū_Mū-Banerjee):
Should any monk have an unrelated nun wash, dye, or beat an old robe, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
NP.5 (PrMoSū_Mū-Banerjee): [The same applies for having her do so] with a new robe.
Furthermore, if a monk should receive a robe from a nun who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).

NP.6. Furthermore, if a monk, having approached a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, should request a robe, except on a specific occasion, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
In this regard, the occasion is as follows: when a monk’s robes have been snatched away, lost, burnt, carried off by water, or stolen—this is the occasion.
For a monk whose robes have been snatched away, lost, burnt, carried off by water, or stolen, [he may accept a robe from] a householder who is not a relative.

A householder’s wife should be requested for a robe. If a faithful brahmin or householder should offer to provide him with an excessive number of robes, that monk, if he so desires, may accept from them at most an inner robe and an upper robe; if he should accept more than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If, with reference to a monk, an unrelated householder or householder’s wife should provide funds for a robe,
thinking, "With these robe-funds, having purchased such and such a robe, [I shall give it] to the monk named so-and-so..."
"A monk will come, and I shall clothe him with a robe, at the proper time and one that is allowable.

In this situation, a certain monk, having previously been uninvited, might entertain some such thought and, approaching a householder or a householder’s wife who are not his relatives, should say: "Those robe-funds which you, venerable sir, have set aside for my sake..."
"Venerable sir, these robe-funds have been set aside for you; having purchased such and such a robe with them, may I clothe you in a robe that is timely and permissible.
If the robe is completed, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Now, it may happen that an unrelated householder and a householder’s wife, with reference to a certain monk,
have each separately set aside funds for the purchase of robes.
"Each of us, with these respective funds for robe-material, having purchased such and such a robe individually, will clothe the monk named so-and-so when he comes;
each of us [will do so] from our respective funds for robe-material, at the proper time and in a permissible manner."

In that case, if that monk, having not been previously invited, should fall into some such deliberation and, approaching that householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative, should say: "Those individual robe-funds which have been set aside for you, venerable lady, intended for yourself..."

"Venerable ones, those two should each, with their respective funds for robes, have robes of such and such a kind made and wear them; both of them, having obtained a single robe each that is timely and permissible, out of a desire for what is beautiful— if the robe is finished, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."

Now, if, with reference to a certain monk, a king, or a royal minister, or a brahmin, or a householder, or a merchant from the city, or a person from the countryside, or a wealthy man, or a guild-leader, or a caravan leader, should send robe-funds by the hand of a messenger:
Then that messenger, taking those provisions, should approach the monk;

having approached him, he should say to that monk: "Venerable sir, you should know that these have been intended for you by a king, or a royal minister, or a brahmin, or a householder, or a merchant from the city, or a person from the countryside, or a wealthy man, or a guild-leader, or a caravan leader."
"Or, may the noble one accept these robe-funds sent by way of this messenger out of compassion.
That monk should say this to the messenger: "Go, venerable messenger; it is permissible for monks to accept robe-funds.
However, we accept a robe only when we have obtained it at the proper time and it is allowable."
That messenger should say this to that monk: "Is there anyone among the noble ones who acts as an attendant, who undertakes service for the noble ones?

A monk desiring robes should designate an attendant, whether a monastery servant (ārāmika) or a lay follower (upāsaka), saying: "O messenger, these are the attendants of the monks; these undertake service for the monks.
Then that messenger, taking those robe-funds, should go to where that attendant is.
Having approached that attendant, one should say this:

"O venerable attendant, you should know that with these robe-funds, having purchased such and such a robe, a monk named so-and-so will come; you should clothe him with that robe at the proper time, provided it is allowable."
Then that messenger, having properly and thoroughly instructed and exhorted that attendant, should go to where that monk is.

Having approached him, he should say to that monk: "Venerable sir, you should go at the appointed time to that attendant whom the noble one has designated and instructed; he will provide you with a robe, provided it is suitable for the season."
A monk who needs a robe should approach the attendant and urge and remind him two or three times, saying:
"I am in need, venerable attendant; I am in need of a robe, venerable attendant.
If that robe is obtained as a result of urging and reminding two or three times, it is well.

If it should not be obtained, one must remain silently in the designated place for four, five, or six times; if, while remaining silently in the designated place for up to four, five, or six times, that robe-cloth should be obtained, that is well. If it is not obtained, one must not seek further nor strive for the acquisition of the robe-cloth once [the limit] has been reached. When the robe-cloth has been obtained...
This is a natural offense of expiation (*naiḥsargika-pāyantikā*).

If it should not be accomplished, one must either go in person to the direction from which those robe-funds were brought, or send a trusted messenger, saying: "Those robe-funds intended for the monk named so-and-so by you, venerable sirs..."
Those [robes] sent after him do not serve any purpose for that monk; let the venerable ones know their own purpose, lest your purpose be lost—this is the rule in that regard.
(NP.11 PrMoSū_Mū-Banerjee)

The seven principles for the settlement of legal cases:
Indeed, Venerable Ones, these seven principles for the settlement of legal cases come up for recitation every half-month during the exposition of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
For one who deserves resolution in the presence [of the accused], we shall grant resolution in the presence.
To one who deserves the *smṛti-vinaya*, we shall grant the *smṛti-vinaya*;
to one who deserves the *amūḍha-vinaya*, we shall grant the *amūḍha-vinaya*;
to one who deserves the *yadbhūyeṣīya*, we shall grant the *yadbhūyeṣīya*.

Venerable ones, the introduction to the recitation of the Prātimokṣasūtra has been recited by me.
The four *pārājika* rules have been recited; the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules; the two *aniyata* rules;

the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyantika* rules; the ninety *pāyantika* rules; the four *pratideśanīya* rules; the numerous *śaikṣa* rules; and the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* rules—this much is [the code] of that Blessed One.
"Whatever has been set forth in the discourses and included within the discourses of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One—

you must apply yourselves with intense mental protection, mindfulness, and heedfulness."
"Patience is the supreme austerity; the Buddhas declare that endurance is the highest [state], for one who harms others is not a renunciant, nor does one who oppresses others become a *śramaṇa*.
Like one with sight [avoiding pitfalls], when there is the power to act,"
In this world of living beings, the wise person should avoid all evil deeds:
refraining from slander and refraining from harming others, and maintaining restraint according to the Prātimokṣa.
Moderation in this food, a secluded dwelling,
and application to the higher mind— this is the instruction of the Buddhas.
Just as a bee, without harming the flower's color or fragrance, [takes its nectar].
Taking only the essence [of his food], the sage should wander thus through the village.
He should not observe the faults of others, nor what others have done or left undone;
rather, he should examine only himself—both his own equanimity and his own failings.
Do not be negligent regarding the higher mind, O Sage, as you train in the stages of silence.
Sorrows do not befall the protector who is ever tranquil and mindful.
For one who gives, merit increases; for one who exercises restraint, enmity does not accumulate.
The virtuous person abandons evil; through the destruction of the afflictions, there is nirvana.
To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome, and to fully subdue one’s own mind—this is the instruction of the Buddhas.
Restraint of the body is good; restraint of speech is also good.
Restraint of the mind is good; restraint in all things is good.
A monk who is restrained in all things is liberated from all suffering.
One should guard one's speech, be well-restrained in mind, and likewise not perform unwholesome deeds with the body.
Having purified these three paths of action, one shall not fail to attain the path proclaimed by the Seers:
the Buddha Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakutsunda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa.
The unsurpassed Śākyamuni Gautama, the god beyond gods, the charioteer who tames men—
by him this Prātimokṣa has been recited in detail for the seven glorious Buddha-heroes, the foremost protectors and lords of the world. (11–12)
In this [teaching], the Buddhas and those who are the disciples of the Buddhas are full of reverence;
having become full of reverence for this, may you attain the unconditioned. (13)
Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket.

Having abandoned the cycle of birth, he will make an end of suffering. (15) This Prātimokṣa, which is worthy of mutual protection through ethical discipline and for the increase of the Teaching, has been recited; the Poṣadha ceremony has been performed by the Saṃgha. (16)
For whose sake this Sūtra was taught, for whose sake the Poṣadha was established—
protect that virtue as a yak protects the tip of its tail.
Whatever merit has been acquired from the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, [may it be for the benefit of all beings].
By this, may this entire world attain the state of the Lord of Sages.
